title: Hershele and the Spoon Medicine
summary: Gray rain falls on Mezhibozh, and Rabbi Baruch sits sadly by the window with a little cloud on his hat. Tea, cake and songs don't help, until Hershele jingles in with pockets full of spoons: "The doctor said one spoon every half hour!" A gentle, funny rhyming story about cheering up someone who is sad.
pages:
A whole day of rain fell on Mezhibozh; the street was gray and wet,
and the Rabbi sat by the window — suddenly as sad as he could get.
On his hat sat a little gray cloud that refused to unstick,
and the room was so quiet you could hear: tick, tick, tick.

The Hasidim brought hot tea, and cake, and a song, and even an orange cat,
but the Rabbi only sighed — and another little cloud landed on his shoulder: boom! Just like that.

Then suddenly — jingle-jingle-jingle! — who's this? Hershele, his pockets puffed out round,
and every step he took jingled like a hundred happy little bells — what a sound!

"What's in your pockets?" they asked, and peeked in. Spoons — quite a few!
"One spoon every half hour — doctor's orders, no joking, it's true!"
He lined them up on the table, from the tiniest to the biggest of all,
and the Rabbi raised one eyebrow: "And that's the whole medicine? That's all?"

Ding-ding! Hershele pulled out a spoon — tsing-tsing! The first spoon, full of golden honey.
The Rabbi tasted, and the sweetness rose right up to his nose — he almost smiled! But... sad again, not sunny.

Ding-ding! Hershele pulled out a spoon — tsing-tsing! The second spoon — he balanced it on the tip of his nose.
It danced, it wobbled — and fell: plop! Down it goes!
And the Rabbi's mustache twitched — was that maybe half a smile?
"Another spoon," said Hershele, "and more, and more — all for you, all the while!"

Ding-ding! Hershele pulled out a spoon — tsing-tsing! The third spoon — he grabbed a pot, and a bowl, and a pail,
and started to drum: rum-pum-tak! The orange cat leaped off the chair, kicked, and ran off with a flick of its tail.
And suddenly the Rabbi's shoe began tapping all on its own: tap-tap-tee!
The Rabbi stared at it, his mustache trembled, and he almost — almost — laughed with glee.

Ding-ding! Hershele pulled out a spoon — tsing-tsing! The fourth spoon, shiny as a mirror, bright.
The Rabbi looked in, and what did he see? A giant nose, a crooked mustache, a long stretched face — "Wow! Is that me? What a sight!"

This time the Rabbi stood up, took a spoon himself, and set it on the tip of his nose,
and stood on one leg — the spoon fell: plop! Down it goes!
And the Rabbi laughed, and laughed, and laughed, and couldn't stop,
until the cloud on his hat vanished, floated away — and was gone: pop!

The Hasidim opened the door — and froze; they couldn't believe their eyes:
the Rabbi on one leg, Hershele on two, and the cat on four — all of them dancing on every leg they had, what a surprise!

The rain stopped, the sun came out, and the puddles sparkled outside,
and the Rabbi sat by the window — this time with a smile on his face, calm and bright-eyed.
And when another half hour had passed — ding-ding! — the Rabbi turned to his friend with a grin,
pulled out a spoon — tsing-tsing! — full of honey. And this time it was for Hershele to dig in!
